summary:
The Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 is in force. It provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality", a category that includes sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18; twenty years' imprisonment for homosexuality or attempted homosexuality; ten years for purporting to contract a same-sex marriage or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony; and three years for a minor convicted of homosexuality. A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in a childcare facility even after release. A provision of the 2023 bill that would have criminalised identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years' imprisonment was proposed but ultimately excluded from the Act.

On 4 April 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties of up to 20 years, and rejected challenges arguing that public participation requirements had not been met. The same court had earlier voided a comparable 2013 statute on procedural grounds, leaving the 2023 Act fully in force.

Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed a constitutional amendment stating "Marriage between persons of the same sex is prohibited."

Enforcement under the Act is documented. In February 2026 police in Arua detained two women after neighbours reported them for kissing in public, one of the first known arrests under the 2023 law. A Human Rights Watch report of 26 May 2025 found that the Act had produced arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings, with many LGBT people in hiding and a small group of Ugandan mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children. In June 2024 a pressure group told Reuters that rights violations against LGBT people were escalating.

Trans-specific violence carries dates in this record. In January 2024 a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false allegation circulated on TikTok, and she was sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house. In June 2021 a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala produced forty-four arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held, and several detainees alleged police performed invasive anal examinations. The most recent documented instance of physical violence against a trans person in this record is January 2024; no later instance is documented.

Digital entrapment is a documented enforcement route. Access Now reported on 15 May 2025 that digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, that the companies behind popular apps do too little, and it published 2025 case research and safety recommendations. Amnesty International reported on 23 October 2024 on doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and found that the 2023 Act fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

Legal gender recognition has one documented instance. In October 2021 trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised. The source does not address any broader document or legal gender recognition process beyond this case.

Outing and state-tolerated hostility have a long documented chain. In October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution, and activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper. The government banned 38 NGOs in June 2012 accused of promoting homosexuality, and Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest. The sources describe discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks and harassment carried out or incited by state officials.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion data is dated and measures different questions. A 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll showed 59 percent agreeing that gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people. Neither figure is current, and neither addresses attitudes toward trans people.

The Guardian reported on 7 January 2024 that the anti-gay laws drew international condemnation while retaining continued political support in parts of Africa, a split that shapes how external pressure is received locally.

A 2011 US State Department Human Rights Report on Uganda listed violence and discrimination against the LGBT community among the three most important problems in the country, during the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates. That assessment predates the 2023 Act.

Health context in the inventory is general rather than trans-specific: Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that abstinence-until-marriage programmes discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and a 2018 article in African Health Sciences traced Uganda's high HIV rate to stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work.
localsOnly:
Residents convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality are barred from employment in childcare facilities even after release, and a minor convicted of homosexuality faces three years' imprisonment.

Amnesty International's 23 October 2024 report, titled "Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names", found that LGBTQ people and organisations have had to change how they present themselves online, including names used, because of the climate created by the 2023 Act.

The June 2021 raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala, with forty-four arrests and allegations of invasive anal examinations by police, documents the treatment of detainees in custody in a shelter setting.

Organisational space is restricted: the government banned 38 NGOs in June 2012 accused of promoting homosexuality, and Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest.

Only one legal gender recognition case is documented, the October 2021 issuance of female identification documents to Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro. No general procedure for changing gender markers on documents is sourced.

Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, and the 2023 Act adds ten years' imprisonment for purporting to contract such a marriage or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony.

Human Rights Watch reported in May 2025 that many LGBT people in the country are in hiding, and that a small group of Ugandan mothers have spoken publicly for their LGBT children.
outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department travel advisory page for Uganda was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). The underlying advisory is reported to include LGBT-specific warnings under its "Do Not Travel" level, but the exact wording of those warnings is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory documents a trans-specific healthcare ban or trans-specific care-access barrier. The 2018 African Health Sciences item addresses HIV and stigma generally and does not address healthcare access for trans people; whether such barriers exist is not sourced.

Beyond the single October 2021 case, no source addresses a general document or legal gender recognition process, so the current administrative route for changing gender markers is unresolved.

No trans-specific killing rate with a denominator is available in the inventory, so no comparative rate against the general homicide rate is stated.

Several claims rest on a single tertiary source and are not independently corroborated within this inventory: the June 2021 shelter raid and anal-examination allegations, the childcare employment ban, the minor's three-year sentence, the 2005 constitutional amendment wording, and the October 2010 tabloid publication.
